blocks.text: Quick verdict

ProxyEmpire is the better value for general scraping and mixed workloads: $3.50/GB at entry against NodeMaven's $4.50/GB pay-as-you-go, free ISP targeting, datacenter and unlimited plans, and a $1.97 trial. NodeMaven is the better choice for social media, multi-accounting and anti-detect browser work, where its IP Quality Filter, long sticky sessions, quality guarantee and $2.20/GB monthly plans reduce bans. Both roll over unused traffic, so irregular usage is safe either way.

NodeMaven and ProxyEmpire both sell residential and mobile proxies on a single system, both keep unused traffic and both have pools of around 30 million advertised IPs. NodeMaven differentiates on IP quality, filtering each IP before assignment with three strictness levels and paying out for bad proxies. ProxyEmpire differentiates on price, free ISP targeting and a broader catalog including datacenter and unlimited residential plans. This comparison helps you choose for scraping and account work.

blocks.text: NodeMaven in 2026: what you get

NodeMaven is the quality-first option. Instead of handing out whatever IP the pool returns, it screens addresses in real time and lets you choose how strict the screening is. That matters most for account-based work such as social media management and multi-accounting, where a flagged IP can cost you an account. The price reflects it: $4.50/GB without a plan and $2.20/GB on monthly plans.

Strengths: IP Quality Filter screens IPs before you get them; Long sticky sessions for account work; Traffic rollover and cashback; Quality guarantee that pays for bad IPs. Weak spots: Smaller pool than mass-market networks; No datacenter proxies; Pay-as-you-go rate is double the plan rate.
ProxyEmpire in 2026: what you get

ProxyEmpire is a Bulgarian-registered provider (SWIFT SAAS LTD) that has been selling since 2020. Its residential and mobile networks share one system with 30M+ advertised IPs in 170+ countries, and country, region, city and ISP targeting are included at no extra cost. The standout policy is bandwidth rollover: prepaid traffic carries forward indefinitely, even after a subscription lapses. Proxyway's 2026 market tests found ProxyEmpire's pool was the third largest among the providers it tested.

Strengths: Prepaid traffic rolls over indefinitely; ISP/ASN targeting included at no extra cost; Cheap $1.97 trial covering residential and mobile; Unlimited residential option priced per day. Weak spots: Smaller advertised pool than the big three; Exact GB thresholds for each tier only shown at checkout; Weaker results on Google in some independent tests.
Pricing: NodeMaven vs ProxyEmpire

NodeMaven charges $4.50/GB pay-as-you-go and $2.20/GB on monthly plans, with residential and mobile traffic on one balance. A $3.50 trial includes 750 MB. Unused traffic rolls over, and you earn up to 10% cashback on used traffic. ISP proxies start at $2.99 per IP with unlimited traffic.

ProxyEmpire's rotating residential pricing currently starts at $3.50/GB (shown as 50% off a $7 list price) and steps down through several tiers to $1.50/GB at 1 TB, with custom pricing from about $0.75/GB above 5 TB. Rotating mobile starts at $4.50/GB, rotating datacenter at about $0.65/GB, and a flat-rate unlimited residential plan is sold by the day.

For a 10 GB month, ProxyEmpire costs about $35 while NodeMaven costs about $45, so ProxyEmpire saves around 22%. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because ProxyEmpire does not publish an exact price for that volume; NodeMaven comes to about $220. Neither provider makes you use it or lose it: both NodeMaven and ProxyEmpire let unused traffic carry forward, so the comparison really comes down to rate and features.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

On paper the two networks are similar in size: NodeMaven advertises 30M+ residential + 250K mobile residential IPs and ProxyEmpire advertises 30M+. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, NodeMaven lists 150+ countries and ProxyEmpire lists 170+. On targeting, NodeMaven offers country, region, city and ISP, while ProxyEmpire offers country, region, city and ISP/ASN (included by default).
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, NodeMaven offers rotating or long sticky sessions (multi-day), and ProxyEmpire offers rotating or sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: stable connections and traffic that never expires. The limitation on the NodeMaven side: the quality filter matters less for high-rotation crawling.

SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. NodeMaven: workable, but you pay a premium for filtering you may not need. ProxyEmpire: Google was its weakest target in independent tests. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Social media and multi-account management: NodeMaven. NodeMaven has the edge here. Why: pre-screened, low-fraud-score IPs with long sticky sessions. How ProxyEmpire compares: residential and mobile IPs with 24-hour sticky sessions.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: free city and ISP targeting. The limitation on the NodeMaven side: fine for light checks.
Ad verification and geo-testing: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: ISP-level targeting at no extra cost. The limitation on the NodeMaven side: good quality but a smaller pool.
Tight budgets: ProxyEmpire wins. The deciding factor for ProxyEmpire: rollover means nothing you pay for is wasted. The limitation on the NodeMaven side: mid-priced on plans, expensive on PAYG.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB. ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile. Verification and payment rules differ too. NodeMaven: Standard. ProxyEmpire: Standard verification. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test NodeMaven and ProxyEmpire before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle NodeMaven vs ProxyEmpire faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (NodeMaven: $3.50 trial with 750 MB; ProxyEmpire: $1.97 trial with 100 MB residential and 50 MB mobile).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.

3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country. 4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, NodeMaven comes out ahead in 1, ProxyEmpire in 4, and 1 is a tie. That makes ProxyEmpire the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: NodeMaven is strongest for social media and multi-account management, while ProxyEmpire is strongest for teams that hate losing unused bandwidth. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
